Salman Rushdie. Born in 1947, a British-Indian novelist whose defiant blending of magical realism, postmodern narrative, and postcolonial critique has established him as a major voice in contemporary literature. His novels collapse historical realism into mythic excess, treat language as performative and unstable, and interrogate the legacies of empire, identity, and cultural hybridity from a diasporic perspective.

Midnight's Children, published in 1981, won the Booker Prize. It narrates the lives of children born at the moment of Indian independence, blending historical epic with magical realism and narrative self-consciousness. The Satanic Verses, from 1988, provoked the Iranian fatwa in 1989 against Rushdie. The novel blends realism and fantasy, addresses migration, identity, and religious hybridity. It became a symbol of free expression versus religious censorship. Rushdie employs magical realism, the seamless integration of fantastic and realistic elements, to represent postcolonial consciousness and the instability of official narratives of history and identity. His prose is digressive, densely allusive, and playful with language. He treats English as a postcolonial inheritance to be stretched, deformed, and made anew. Shame, published in 1983, is an allegorical political novel set in a fictional South Asian nation, combining satire, family saga, and metafiction. His work foregrounds diaspora, migration, and the construction of identity across cultural borders. He writes from exile, both forced and chosen, with sympathy for the displaced. Rushdie synthesizes postcolonial concerns with postmodern narrative techniques through magical realism, as does Zadie Smith, another postcolonial novelist who blends exuberant narrative with social critique.
